Emma Lazarus. An American poet and essayist who lived from eighteen forty-nine to eighteen eighty-seven, and whose most famous work became the defining poem of American immigration itself. She died young of Hodgkin lymphoma at thirty-eight, but the words she left behind have echoed through generations.

She wrote "The New Colossus" in eighteen eighty-three as a sonnet commissioned for the Statue of Liberty, and her phrase "your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free" now defines how America sees itself. Those words are inscribed on the monument's base, inseparable from what the statue means. She worked in multiple poetic modes: translations of Hebrew verse, dramatic monologues, philosophical meditations on suffering and redemption.

In eighteen seventy-four she published Songs of a Semite, a collection centered on Jewish identity written after Russian pogroms renewed her commitment to her heritage. She was intellectually ambitious, studying languages, translating from Hebrew and German, engaging seriously with both classical and contemporary literature. Her poetry combined classical rigor with moral urgency.

So here's the strange thing: her fame for "The New Colossus" came mostly after her death, when immigration became the defining question of American identity. She's become the poet of immigration itself, the voice that speaks for those rejected elsewhere. Her invocation of the huddled masses defines the mythology we've built around who America is. Her poetry and her activism together shaped how we think about refuge and welcome, even though few people ever know her name.
